note.insufficient: Not enough events yet to separate growth from volatility. With 3+ events this reading becomes reliable.
note.stable: Even performance event to event: what you show is what you are. To move up a tier you have to shift the average, not the variance.
note.growthLag: Your spread is growth, not inconsistency: the trend explains {r2Pct}% of it. The real problem is that your season OPR runs {scoutingGap} points behind your current form — and captains scout you on that lagging number.
note.growthClear: Clear growth trend (+{slope} OPR per event). The lever is holding the slope, not reducing variance.
note.decline: The trend is heading down ({slope} OPR per event). Before optimizing anything, find what degraded: mechanical wear, late design changes, or progressively stronger fields.
note.volatility: Your spread is noise, not trend: the line only explains {r2Pct}% of it, so every event is a coin flip between {min} and {max} OPR. The lever is raising the floor (failures, reliability), not the ceiling.
note.mixed: A mix of growth and noise: the trend explains {r2Pct}% of your spread and the rest is real volatility (±{residualSigma} OPR). Worth attacking both fronts.

SeasonAnalysis.title: Season Analysis
SeasonAnalysis.desc: The season read live from official results: how the team's output moved event to event, how much of that movement is a trend rather than noise, and what it means for alliance selection.
SeasonAnalysis.methodology: Per-event values are the team's average net points (score minus fouls) in qualification matches — the app's stand-in for OPR. It credits the whole alliance's output to the team, so it runs high compared with a least-squares OPR: read it as a within-team trend across this season, not as a figure comparable between teams.

strategy.topOrdered: Ordered field and you're up top: results tend to respect OPR. Ideal.
strategy.topChaotic: You're up top but the field is volatile: favorite with upset risk — lock in your seed during quals.
strategy.topTypical: Competitive position in a typical field: your quals seed decides your luck.
strategy.bubbleChaotic: Bubble zone in a chaotic field: upsets are common — a good day gets you into playoffs.
strategy.bubbleTypical: Bubble zone: you need an above-average event to make playoffs.
strategy.outChaoticUpside: Strong but volatile field: tough, though the chaos gives more openings than an ordered field.
strategy.outAboveLevel: Field above your current level: valuable as experience, unlikely for playoffs.

autoTeleopLevers.title: Auto raises the ceiling; teleop raises the floor
autoTeleopLevers.body: They're two different levers, not one. Auto is the weakest point by level (top {autoTopPct}% worldwide vs. top {teleopEndgameTopPct}% in teleop/endgame) and it's already growing steadily (+{autoSlope} OPR per event): that's where the most world rank is gained. Teleop is the opposite case — strong level but the season's most unstable phase (±{teleopNoise} OPR of noise the trend doesn't explain). There, the win isn't ceiling — it's consistency.

publicNumberLag.title: The public season number lags real form
publicNumberLag.body: The season OPR ({seasonOpr}) averages the early events and sits {gap} points below current form ({currentForm}). Since captains scout on that number, the gap costs draft position: the lever isn't reducing variance — it's making recent form visible.

nextTier.title: The next step is the veteran tier ({veteranFloor}+ OPR)

rpAndSeed.title: RP bonuses and seed are worth gold
rpAndSeed.body: In double elimination, a top-4 seed is worth disproportionately more because of the byes. Being 'pickable' to top captains (consistent, visible auto) outweighed two ranking spots at FPEMX — the PRIDE model called {correct} of {total} playoffs correctly.

CalibrationDashboard.adminOnly: Section visible only to team admins/leads.
CalibrationDashboard.tipBody: Brier measures mean squared error: lower = better, 0.25 = guessing, <0.15 = excellent. The reliability diagram shows whether "70% prob" really hits ~70% of the time. It needs generated predictions (briefings) + matches played + ground-truth validation running.
CalibrationDashboard.title: Model calibration
CalibrationDashboard.subtitle: How reliable the simulator's and scouts' predictions are.
CalibrationDashboard.scoutReliabilityHint: Computed by ground-truth validation against official scores. Update by running the validator in the sidebar.
CalibrationDashboard.diagramHint: Each bar = bucket of predictions. The empirical height should approach the "perfect" diagonal line.
CalibrationDashboard.emptyStep1: You generate match briefings (each one is logged automatically)
CalibrationDashboard.emptyStep2: The matches are played and the official scores show up in the FTC API
CalibrationDashboard.emptyStep3: You run the ground-truth validator from the sidebar
CalibrationDashboard.explainBrier: Brier score = mean squared error between predicted probability and outcome (0/1). A model that always predicts 0.5 scores 0.25; a perfect model scores 0. Statbotics reports ~0.18 for FRC.
CalibrationDashboard.explainLogLoss: Log loss = penalty for confidence in wrong answers. More sensitive than Brier to "100% sure but lost". Lower = better.
CalibrationDashboard.explainAccuracy: Accuracy = % of matches where the alliance with ≥50% probability actually won. Measures binary predictive power; ignores confidence.
CalibrationDashboard.explainDiagram: Reliability diagram = if you say "70% prob", you should be right ~70% of the time. Tall bars in low buckets = underconfidence; short bars in high buckets = overconfidence.

OraclePage.metaDescription: PRIDE's prediction model, validated against {matches} real playoff matches across {seasons} seasons. Accuracy, error and calibration published in the open.
OraclePage.heroBody: PRIDE predicts playoff winners. This page publishes how often it is right — and, more importantly, whether its probabilities mean what they say. Everything was recalculated from real matches; nothing is rounded in its favor.
OraclePage.relLead: Accuracy alone is not enough. If the model says "80% probability", those matches should be won 8 times out of 10 — no more, no less. This is what happened across the {matches} playoff matches of 2024 and 2025.
OraclePage.badFirstBody: The original model estimated its uncertainty from qualification matches. In playoffs that turned out far too optimistic: when it said 98% it won {p98}% of the time, and when it said 85% it won {p85}%. It looked sure of things it should not have been.
OraclePage.fixTitle: The fix was learned from the data
OraclePage.fixBody: In elimination the real uncertainty is 2.4× larger than in qualification — a number fitted on these same matches, not picked by hand. With that correction every bucket falls within 3 points of what was realized.
OraclePage.relNote: Each column has its own match count because the buckets don't hold the same matches in both models: correcting the uncertainty moves predictions from the high buckets toward the center — the 90-100% bucket goes from {from} to {to} matches. That is exactly what it means to stop exaggerating certainty.
OraclePage.seasonsLead: Every FTC season is a new game, with its own rules and way of scoring. The same model, without re-tuning per season, stays in the same band — a sign it generalizes by design and not by chance.
OraclePage.howToRead: How to read it. Brier measures the error of the probability (0 is perfect; 0.25 equals always saying 50/50). Calibration is the stated confidence minus the achieved accuracy: negative means the model was somewhat more pessimistic than necessary. Power Play (2022) is the low point in accuracy, and it is explainable: it was a defensive-meta season, and defense doesn't show up in an offensive metric. That is exactly the gap human scouting fills.
OraclePage.powerPlayNote: Worth noting that that same season had the tightest calibration of the seven ({gap} pp): the model was right less often, but it did not oversell. It lost accuracy, not honesty.
OraclePage.levelTitle: The more even the field, the harder it is
OraclePage.levelLead: The same model loses accuracy as the event level rises. It is not a defect: at Worlds every team is strong, so the difference between alliances is smaller and the result depends more on what no model sees.
OraclePage.limitsLead: The limits matter as much as the hits.
OraclePage.limit1Title: It does not predict individual qualification matches
OraclePage.limit1Body: Everything on this page is about playoffs, where the alliances are already formed. Qualification matches have different dynamics and were not evaluated here.
OraclePage.limit2Title: It measures offensive power, not strategy
OraclePage.limit2Body: The model starts from how much each team scores. An alliance that wins through defense, a tiebreaking autonomous or human coordination looks worse than it is. Power Play shows it.
OraclePage.limit3Title: A 76% leaves 1 in 4 matches on the other side
OraclePage.limit3Body: It is a tool for deciding better, not an oracle. Any team that uses it to stop scouting is using it backwards.
OraclePage.limit4Body: The public FTCScout API was used. Events without published results were left out of the calculation, and seasons before 2019 were not included because they don't exist there.
OraclePage.verifyBody: No figure on this page was written by hand: they all come from running the backtest against the public API and recalculating. Anyone can repeat it.
OraclePage.footer: PRIDE · Iron Lion Robotics (FTC #30311) · Monterrey, Mexico
OraclePage.chartAria: Reliability diagram. The original model sits below the diagonal (overconfidence): when it predicts 98% it wins {p98}%. The corrected model follows the diagonal within 3 points in every bucket.
